title: Compass Correlations in a Square-Lattice Magnet
authors: Otkur Omar, Matthias D. Frontzek, Gabriele Sala, Junying Shen, Xinmin Wang, Ze Hu, Zhuang Xu, Zecong Qin, Xin Tong, Joe Paddison, Max Hirschberger, Shinichiro Seki, Masaaki Matsuda, Matthew B. Stone, Andrew D. Christianson, Nguyen D. Khanh, Shang Gao
abstract: The square-lattice compass model is a paradigm of bond-dependent frustration, yet experimental evidence for its characteristic spin correlations has remained elusive. Here we identify compass correlations in the square-lattice intermetallic ErRu$_2$Si$_2$ using single-crystal neutron diffuse scattering. Comparative measurements on the isostructural compounds NdRu$_2$Si$_2$ and ErRu$_2$Si$_2$ reveal a pronounced contrast between nearly uniform diffuse rings in the former and strong intensity modulation between Brillouin zones in the latter. Through the magnetic neutron polarization factor, this modulation reveals compass correlations that couple moment orientation to the correlation wavevector. Crystal-field spectroscopy identifies four preferred in-plane orientations for the Er$^{3+}$ moments. A minimal compass-Heisenberg model incorporating this anisotropy quantitatively reproduces the diffuse scattering and accounts for the double-$Q$ vortex-antivortex ground state. Fits with the compass couplings fixed at values set by the dipolar energy scale retain good agreement with the data, supporting a substantial dipolar contribution to the bond-dependent interactions. Our results establish a square-lattice platform for compass physics and suggest that dipolar interactions, acting together with local crystal-field anisotropy, can shape directional magnetic correlations alongside conduction-electron-mediated exchange.
summary: This paper reports the experimental detection of compass correlations in the magnet $	ext{ErRu}_2	ext{Si}_2$ using neutron scattering. By comparing it to a similar compound, the authors show that the correlations are directional, which they model using a compass-Heisenberg Hamiltonian. The results strongly suggest that dipolar interactions, constrained by local crystal fields, are crucial in shaping these complex magnetic patterns.
main_problem: The study aims to experimentally identify and theoretically model compass correlations in the square-lattice magnet $	ext{ErRu}_2	ext{Si}_2$, where direct evidence for these correlations has been difficult to obtain.
main_result: The authors successfully identified compass correlations in $	ext{ErRu}_2	ext{Si}_2$ using neutron scattering, showing that dipolar interactions, combined with local crystal-field anisotropy, are key in shaping these directional magnetic correlations.
method: The research combines single-crystal neutron diffuse scattering experiments with theoretical fitting using a minimal compass-Heisenberg model.
model_or_system: The system is the rare-earth intermetallic $	ext{ErRu}_2	ext{Si}_2$, modeled by a compass-Heisenberg Hamiltonian that incorporates bond-dependent interactions and local crystal-field anisotropy derived from spectroscopy.
key_observables: Diffuse neutron scattering patterns, specifically the strong intensity modulation between Brillouin zones in $	ext{ErRu}_2	ext{Si}_2$ compared to the uniform rings in $	ext{NdRu}_2	ext{Si}_2$.
important_parameters: Dipolar energy scale, crystal-field parameters ($B_n^k$), and the resulting double-$Q$ vortex-antivortex ground state.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed correlations can be quantitatively described by a minimal compass-Heisenberg model, and that dipolar interactions provide a plausible microscopic origin for the compass couplings.
figures_summary: Figures compare diffuse scattering maps for $	ext{NdRu}_2	ext{Si}_2$ (rings) and $	ext{ErRu}_2	ext{Si}_2$ (modulated arcs), and show the $\chi^2$ landscape mapping to a double-$Q$ vortex-antivortex lattice.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the experimental challenge, presents the comparative neutron scattering data for two isostructural compounds, develops and fits the compass-Heisenberg model to the $	ext{ErRu}_2	ext{Si}_2$ data, and concludes by linking the findings to the role of dipolar interactions.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, measurable platform (the square-lattice magnet) to study directional magnetic correlations driven by competing interactions (dipolar vs. exchange), which is highly relevant to understanding frustrated magnetism in correlated materials.
